title: Renaissance and Enlightenment: Europe's Long Revolution of the Mind

questions.question: The Renaissance began in Italy primarily because of:
options: Trade wealth of city-states, Roman ruins, and Byzantine scholars bringing Greek manuscripts
The Black Death's absence from Italy
questions.rationale: Medici and Venetian wealth funded art and learning; Roman antiquity lay at hand; and after 1453 Greek scholars fleeing Constantinople carried classical texts west — Italy held every ingredient of the rebirth.

questions.question: Petrarch is called 'the father of humanism' for:
options: Recovering and championing classical Latin texts and human-centred learning
questions.rationale: Petrarch's recovery of Cicero and the classical tradition — studying human letters (studia humanitatis) rather than scholastic theology — set the movement's agenda. Gutenberg did the printing, Michelangelo the ceiling, Copernicus the heavens.

questions.question: Which invention most accelerated the spread of both the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution?
questions.rationale: Printing (c. 1455) made books and pamphlets cheap: Luther's theses went viral, vernacular Bibles spread literacy, and scientific journals travelled between scholars — the era's information infrastructure.

questions.question: Machiavelli's The Prince departed from medieval political thought by:
options: Defending the divine right of kings
Analysing power as it is, separating politics from morality
questions.rationale: Machiavelli studied statecraft empirically — how rulers gain and keep power — without grounding it in religion or ethics, founding modern political science.

questions.question: The phrase 'life, liberty, and property' as natural rights the state must protect is associated with:
questions.rationale: Locke's Two Treatises argued that governments exist by consent to protect natural rights, and may be overthrown when they breach the trust. Jefferson adapted the trio to 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness' in 1776.

questions.question: The separation of powers into legislative, executive, and judicial branches derives from:
options: Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws
questions.rationale: Montesquieu argued that concentrated power invites abuse, so liberty requires checks and balances across three branches — the engineering principle behind the US Constitution.

questions.question: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' opens which work, arguing for popular sovereignty?
questions.rationale: Rousseau's Social Contract (1762) grounded legitimate authority in the general will of the people — the intellectual dynamite under the French Revolution. Leviathan is Hobbes' absolutist counterpoint.

questions.question: Newton's Principia (1687) mattered to the Enlightenment because:
options: It proved the Church correct about astronomy
It showed one law governs both heavens and earth — nature as a knowable machine
It translated the Bible into French
questions.rationale: Universal gravitation unified Kepler's orbits and falling apples under one law. If reason could decode the heavens, Enlightenment thinkers reasoned it could decode society, kings included.

questions.question: Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) argued:
options: The Revolution's rights-logic applies equally to women
questions.rationale: Wollstonecraft turned the Enlightenment's own principles against its blind spot: if rights rest on reason, and women possess reason, denying them education and rights is incoherent tyranny.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly orders these events?
options: French Revolution - American Declaration - Gutenberg press - Luther's theses
Gutenberg press - Luther's theses - American Declaration - French Revolution
Luther's theses - Gutenberg press - French Revolution - American Declaration
American Declaration - Luther's theses - Gutenberg press - French Revolution
questions.rationale: Printing (c. 1455) armed Luther (1517); the ideas matured through the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment into the American Declaration (1776) and then the French Revolution (1789) — technology to faith to politics.
